item.text: {"question_id":"8B.9","answer":"During 2023, Scholz’s government actively managed multiple crises and generally preserved parts of its stated objectives, but control and demonstrated effects were uneven. In Ukraine, it moved from initial hesitation to substantial, allied-coordinated deliveries of air-defence systems, artillery, armoured vehicles, tanks, training, logistics, and planned winter support, while explicitly balancing Ukrainian defence against avoiding NATO-Russia escalation; the supplied record does not establish that the chosen military objectives were achieved or that escalation was prevented (BATCH-0026-E004; BATCH-0016-E002; BATCH-0016-E005; BATCH-0033-E011). The January Leopard process also shows institutional and coalition resistance: Scholz was still resisting delivery on 19 January, and opponents described the government as delayed, while the governing side characterized coordination as necessary and ultimately defended the planned delivery (BATCH-0031-E001; BATCH-0029-E010). In the Israel-Hamas crisis, Scholz directly pursued hostage release, regional de-escalation, humanitarian access, and protection of Israel through contacts with Israel, Egypt, Türkiye, Qatar, and Jordan; hostages were released during the period and officials credited confidential diplomacy, but the evidence does not establish Scholz’s causal contribution, broader de-escalation, or civilian protection. Germany’s military support for Israel, abstention from a UN ceasefire resolution, and limited public condemnation of reported Israeli violations materially qualify the response (BATCH-0029-E007; BATCH-0031-E002; BATCH-0033-E011; BATCH-0011-R04-E005; BATCH-0008-E016). In Niger, the government supported ECOWAS and African Union mediation, kept diplomatic channels open, treated force as a last resort, and sought restoration of constitutional order, although the outcome and Scholz’s personal role in each decision are not established (BATCH-0032-E008; BATCH-0032-E009). It also organized a concrete Slovenian flood response through THW personnel, equipment, mobile bridges, and €700,000 in financing, though final effectiveness is not reported (BATCH-0032-E008). On migration, the government introduced asylum-procedure reform, independent counselling, strengthened border controls, expanded federal funding, and pursued faster procedures and returns. Yet implementation was delayed, counselling funding was insufficient, border controls were criticized as shifting routes and restricting access, reception capacity was severely strained, and failed removals substantially exceeded effective removals; much of the operational failure lay with Länder and municipalities, limiting direct attribution to Scholz (BATCH-0011-R01-E003; BATCH-0011-R01-E013; BATCH-0011-R04-E013; BATCH-0011-R04-E014; BATCH-0011-R05-E005). Energy measures and gas-price brakes, together with a mild winter, limited economic disruption, but the Constitutional Court ruling invalidated the prior budgetary approach. Scholz accepted the Court’s authority, froze some Climate and Transformation Fund spending, deferred 2024 budget decisions, and proposed a supplementary 2023 budget and emergency authorization for energy relief and flood aid; the supplied period ends before final enactment or implementation, while €60 billion in planned climate and industrial investment was put at risk (BATCH-0016-E016; BATCH-0016-E017; BATCH-0008-E018; BATCH-0024-E013; BATCH-0034-R12-E001). Overall, the record supports active, sometimes coordinated crisis management and partial preservation of objectives, but delays, legal failure, capacity strain, unresolved outcomes, and substantial dependence on allies and subnational actors prevent a consistently effective conclusion. Moral approval or disapproval of these objectives does not affect this execution
